description: A fast-growing evergreen tree up to 15-20 m with a dense rounded crown, pinnate leaves with serrated leaflets, small fragrant white flower clusters and yellowish olive-like fruits (nimboli). All parts are intensely bitter.
cultural_significance: Called the 'village pharmacy' of India. Neem leaves are eaten on Gudi Padwa and Ugadi in a bitter-sweet mix symbolising life's flavours, and twigs are traditionally used as datun (chewing sticks). Not a Vedic-era plant by name with certainty; prominent in the Samhitas and Nighantus.
habitat: Hardy tropical tree of dry and semi-arid plains; tolerates poor soil and drought; planted along roads, villages and temples across India.

uses.title: Skin disorders and itching
uses.detail: Leaf paste and decoctions are traditionally applied or taken for kushtha (skin diseases), acne, boils and itching; it is described as Raktashodhaka (blood purifier).

uses.title: Oral and dental care
uses.detail: Fresh twigs are chewed as datun in rural India to clean teeth and keep gums healthy.

uses.title: Fever and intestinal worms
uses.detail: Bark and leaf preparations are traditionally given as Jvarahara and Krimighna (anti-worm) remedies.

uses.title: Hair and scalp care
uses.detail: Leaf rinses and neem oil are traditionally used for dandruff and head lice.

uses.title: Blood-sugar and antimicrobial research
uses.detail: Laboratory studies on neem extracts report antibacterial, antifungal and glucose-lowering activity; human evidence is limited.

preparations.name: Leaf paste (lepa)
preparations.method: Grind fresh leaves with a little water and apply to the affected skin area.
preparations.note: Patch test first; used externally for boils and itching.

preparations.name: Kwatha (decoction)
preparations.method: Boil leaves or bark in water and strain; used as a wash or taken under guidance.
preparations.note: Very bitter; internal use should be short and supervised.

preparations.name: Neem oil
preparations.method: Oil pressed from the seeds, used diluted on skin and scalp.
preparations.note: For external use only; never swallow.

preparations.name: Datun (chewing twig)
preparations.method: Chew the end of a fresh twig to form a soft brush and clean the teeth.

precautions: Neem seed oil is toxic if swallowed and is especially dangerous for infants and children. Traditionally avoided in pregnancy and by those trying to conceive, as it is described as anti-fertility in high use. May lower blood sugar, so people on diabetes medicines should consult a doctor. Prolonged internal use of leaf or bark may be drying and aggravate Vata.

cultivation.climate: Hot tropical to subtropical; drought tolerant, frost-sensitive when young
cultivation.soil: Well-drained sandy or loamy soil; tolerates poor, rocky ground
cultivation.water: Low; water young plants regularly, mature trees need little
cultivation.propagation: Fresh seeds (lose viability quickly) or root suckers and cuttings
cultivation.harvest: Leaves year-round; fruits collected when yellow in summer-monsoon

fun_fact: Neem twigs have served as natural toothbrushes in India for centuries, and the tree's name in Sanskrit, Arishta, means 'reliever of sickness'.

regions.name: South Asia (Widely cultivated)
regions.note: Planted in villages, roadsides and temples across the subcontinent

regions.name: Deccan Plateau
regions.note: Thrives in the dry plateau climate
